title: Creme Brulee
subtitle: silky vanilla custard with a caramelised sugar crust
excerpt: Creme brulee is custard baked in a water bath until set, then finished with a thin layer of caramelised sugar cracked with a spoon. The contrast between the brittle top and the cold, trembling custard underneath is what makes it extraordinary.
sourceNotes: A classic French dessert. The name means 'burnt cream'. Contested between France, Spain (crema catalana), and England (Cambridge burnt cream).

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Bake the custards up to 2 days ahead and refrigerate. Brulee just before serving.
recipe.temperatureNote: Conventional oven, baked in a water bath

content.text: The water bath (bain-marie) is what prevents the custard from curdling. The water cannot exceed 100C, which keeps the custard temperature gentle throughout the bake. The custard should still wobble in the centre when you take it out -- it will set fully as it chills.

items.prepNote: plus 4 tsp for the bruleed tops
or 1 vanilla pod, split and scraped

content.text: Heat the oven to 150C. Place 4 ramekins in a deep roasting tin.

Heat the cream with the vanilla until just below boiling. Whisk the egg yolks and 80g sugar together in a bowl until pale. Slowly pour the hot cream into the egg mixture, whisking constantly. Do not rush this or the eggs will scramble.
Skim any foam from the surface. Pour the custard through a sieve into a jug. Divide evenly between the ramekins.

Pour hot water into the roasting tin to come halfway up the sides of the ramekins. Transfer carefully to the oven. Bake for 40 to 45 minutes until the custard is just set with a slight wobble in the centre.

Remove from the water bath and cool to room temperature. Refrigerate for at least 4 hours. To brulee: sprinkle 1 tsp caster sugar evenly over each ramekin. Use a kitchen blowtorch to caramelise the sugar until dark amber. Serve immediately.

items.cause: Hot cream was added too quickly to the eggs, or the oven was too hot.
items.fix: Pour the cream in a very thin, slow stream, whisking constantly. A water bath at 150C prevents overcooking.

items.cause: Layer was too thick, or sugar was not spread flat.
items.fix: Use exactly 1 tsp per ramekin. Tap the ramekin to level the sugar before torching. Work in slow circles with the torch.

content.text: Creme brulee is a French restaurant classic that became a British dinner party staple in the 1980s and 90s and has never left. Its appeal is the performance as much as the taste -- the crack of the sugar crust is one of the great moments in dessert. Trinity College Cambridge claims an English version, Cambridge burnt cream, as even older. The debate continues.
